name: Riyadh
meta_description: TDSC investigative consulting in matters touching Riyadh: counterparty diligence, SCCA arbitration support, giga-project and procurement integrity reviews.
hero_lede: Riyadh is Saudi Arabia's capital and the centre of its government, finance and Vision 2030 investment programme. TDSC scopes Riyadh matters around lawful public sources, Saudi privacy and cybercrime restrictions and the city's arbitration institutions, coordinating Saudi counsel and qualified local professionals where the work requires it.
intro: Riyadh is the capital of Saudi Arabia and its largest city, the seat of the royal court, ministries and most national regulators. The Ministry of Economy and Planning's DataSaudi service gives the Riyadh region a population of about 8.59 million in 2022, and the region's registered workforce is concentrated in construction, administrative and support services and trade. The Saudi Central Bank, the Capital Market Authority, the Saudi Exchange and the Public Investment Fund are based in the city, and the King Abdullah Financial District houses many banks and investment firms. Large state-backed developments, the planned Expo 2030 and a government policy encouraging multinationals to base regional headquarters in Riyadh have drawn foreign companies and advisers to the city.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Riyadh because that is where most large Saudi contracts are awarded, financed and disputed. Foreign contractors, suppliers and investors need to understand Saudi partners, agents and sponsors, including their ownership, connections to officials and litigation history, before committing to joint ventures or major projects. Infrastructure, construction and giga-project supply chains raise procurement integrity and subcontractor risk. Disputes are increasingly resolved through arbitration seated in Riyadh, which brings demand for research on parties and assets. Saudi law places firm limits on surveillance, recording and publication of personal information, so the method of inquiry must be settled with Saudi counsel before work begins.

matters.title: Saudi partner and agent diligence
matters.text: Researching Riyadh-based partners, distributors, agents and sponsors before joint ventures, distribution agreements or bids, using commercial registration data, court and enforcement information where available, media and open sources in Arabic and English, and testing for undisclosed links to officials or state entities.

matters.title: Giga-project subcontractor and procurement reviews
matters.text: Reviewing subcontractors, consultants and suppliers on large Riyadh construction and development projects for ownership, capability, related-party links and adverse history, supporting compliance and contracts teams who must manage bribery and conflict-of-interest risk in fast-moving, multi-tier procurement programmes.

matters.title: Arbitration and dispute support
matters.text: Supporting counsel in arbitrations administered by the Saudi Center for Commercial Arbitration in Riyadh and in Saudi court proceedings, with background research on opposing parties, witnesses and experts, and identification of assets and corporate relationships relevant to enforcement.

matters.title: Regional headquarters and market entry
matters.text: Helping companies establishing regional headquarters or first operations in Riyadh to assess local service providers, landlords, recruiters and prospective senior hires, so that early relationships are built on verified information rather than on introductions and reputation alone.

matters.title: Internal fraud and misconduct inquiries
matters.text: Assisting multinational employers with Riyadh offices where expense fraud, kickbacks or conflicts of interest are suspected, scoping document review and interviews with Saudi counsel so that the inquiry respects local labour, privacy and cybercrime law.

local_context.title: Courts in Riyadh
local_context.text: Riyadh hosts the Supreme Court, appeal courts and first-instance courts, including a commercial court that hears disputes between merchants, company disputes and bankruptcy matters, as well as enforcement courts. Saudi enforcement courts have processed about 35,000 applications to enforce arbitral awards since the 2012 Arbitration Law, according to figures cited by the Minister of Justice. Proceedings are conducted in Arabic, and court strategy is a matter for Saudi counsel.

local_context.title: Saudi Center for Commercial Arbitration
local_context.text: The SCCA was established by Council of Ministers decision in 2014 and opened in Riyadh in 2016; its hearing facilities are in the chambers of commerce building in the city. Its 2023 Arbitration Rules allow remote procedural hearings, foreign lawyers, non-Arabic proceedings and arbitrators of any nationality. The 2012 Arbitration Law is based on the UNCITRAL Model Law. The SCCA opened an office in the Dubai International Financial Centre in 2022.

local_context.title: Regulators and integrity bodies
local_context.text: Riyadh is home to the Saudi Central Bank, the Capital Market Authority and the Saudi Exchange, so listed-company disclosures, regulatory announcements and enforcement notices for the whole market originate there. The Oversight and Anti-Corruption Authority, known as Nazaha, is also based in the city and announces corruption cases involving public officials and businesspeople, which are a relevant source for procurement and partner reviews.

local_context.title: Records and practical limits
local_context.text: Commercial registration is administered nationally by the Ministry of Commerce, and basic registration details of Riyadh companies can be checked through official channels, though shareholder and beneficial ownership information is more limited than in many markets. Court records are not generally open for public search. Saudi law penalises invasion of privacy through camera devices and online defamation, so surveillance-style inquiries are not part of TDSC's scope in Riyadh.

tdsc_approach: TDSC handles Riyadh matters from Nashville and has no office, staff or licence in Saudi Arabia. Engagements begin with a review, with the client's Saudi counsel, of what can lawfully be done: which official registration data, regulatory disclosures, Nazaha announcements, court judgments that are published, and Arabic and English media can be used, and which inquiries should not be made. Where local knowledge is needed, TDSC coordinates qualified Saudi professionals working within their legal permissions, and does not use covert recording, pretexting or access to restricted systems. Reports, often for use in SCCA arbitration or compliance decisions, separate documented facts from inference, and personal data is handled with Saudi data protection law in mind.

faqs.q: Is Riyadh a seat for international arbitration?
faqs.a: Yes. The Saudi Center for Commercial Arbitration is headquartered in Riyadh and administers cases under its 2023 Arbitration Rules, which allow non-Arabic proceedings, foreign counsel and arbitrators of any nationality. The 2012 Arbitration Law follows the UNCITRAL Model Law. TDSC does not advise on seat selection but supports research for Riyadh-seated proceedings.

faqs.q: Can we check who owns a Riyadh company?
faqs.a: Basic commercial registration details are available through Ministry of Commerce channels, and listed companies disclose more through the Saudi Exchange. Shareholder and beneficial ownership information for private companies is harder to obtain, so research often combines registration data with media, litigation and open sources, with clear statements about what could not be confirmed.

faqs.q: Does TDSC conduct surveillance in Riyadh?
faqs.a: No. Saudi law treats invasion of privacy through camera-equipped devices and online defamation as offences, and we have not identified a licensing regime for private investigators. TDSC limits Riyadh work to lawful research, analysis and, where appropriate, inquiries by qualified local professionals agreed with Saudi counsel.

faqs.q: Why do giga-project suppliers need diligence?
faqs.a: Large Riyadh developments involve many layers of subcontractors and consultants, often appointed quickly. Compliance teams need to know who owns them, whether they are connected to decision-makers, and whether they have the capacity claimed. Reviews of ownership, related parties, adverse media and Nazaha announcements help manage bribery, fraud and delivery risk.

faqs.q: Which bodies in Riyadh publish enforcement information?
faqs.a: The Capital Market Authority and the Saudi Exchange publish market disclosures and enforcement notices, the Saudi Central Bank regulates banks and insurers, and Nazaha announces corruption cases involving officials and businesspeople. These are useful sources for partner and procurement reviews, alongside Saudi court judgments where they are published.
